overview.title: Prompting SAM with a point and reading its mask outputs
overview.subsection: 11.3.4 Prompting the model with a target point
overview.main_topic: Running Segment Anything (SAM) with a single foreground point prompt, inspecting the shape of the returned masks, and converting one mask into a full-resolution boolean array for display.
overview.central_idea: A SAM call takes a batch of images plus a batch of labeled points and returns four 256 × 256 candidate masks (with predicted IoU scores); a small helper picks one mask, upsamples it to the 1024 × 1024 padded image frame and thresholds it at 0 to get a boolean mask.
overview.importance: This is the first page where the pretrained segmentation model is actually invoked. It shows the exact input dictionary SAM expects, the batch-axis convention, the structure of the output, and the post-processing needed to go from raw model output (low-resolution logits) to a usable pixel mask. The same pattern is reused for every later prompt in the chapter (banana on p.349-350, box on p.351-352).
learning_objectives: Write the input dictionary (`images`, `points`, `labels`) for a SAM point prompt and explain why each array gets a leading batch axis.
Interpret the output shape `(1, 4, 256, 256)` axis by axis.
Explain what the `iou_pred` field contains and how it relates to the IoU metric from p.340.
Explain each line of `get_mask()`: indexing, adding a channel axis, resizing to the image frame, thresholding at 0.
Recognise why the mask must be resized with the same `resize_and_pad` function used for the image.
prerequisites: The SAM architecture: image encoder, prompt encoder, mask decoder (p.344-345)
The `resize_and_pad` helper that maps the photo to a padded 1024 × 1024 frame (p.346)
Intersection over Union (IoU), defined on p.340

summary:
The page opens with **Figure 11.10**, the 1024 × 1024 padded test image (black bars top and bottom from `resize_and_pad`, p.346) with a green star marking the prompt point `(580, 450)` defined on p.347. The point lands on a peach in the fruit bowl.

The authors then call the pretrained model with `model.predict(...)`, passing a dictionary with three entries: `"images"`, `"points"` and `"labels"`. Each array is wrapped with `ops.expand_dims(..., axis=0)` so that it carries a leading **batch axis** of size 1: SAM, like every Keras model, processes batches, even when the batch holds a single image and a single prompt.

The returned value `outputs` is a dictionary. Its `"masks"` entry holds **four 256 × 256 candidate masks** for the object indicated by the prompt; the book says they are ranked by decreasing match quality, and that the model's own quality estimate for each mask is in the `"iou_pred"` field. The shape check `outputs["masks"].shape` prints `(1, 4, 256, 256)`: batch of 1, 4 candidates, 256 × 256 pixels each.

Finally, the page defines a helper `get_mask(sam_outputs, index=0)` that

1. picks the first (only) batch element and the requested candidate,
2. adds a trailing channel axis so the mask looks like an image `(256, 256, 1)`,
3. resizes it with `resize_and_pad` to the same `1024 × 1024` frame as the image, and
4. converts it to NumPy and thresholds it with `> 0.0`, producing a boolean mask.

The page ends by calling `mask = get_mask(outputs, index=0)`; the resulting overlay (Figure 11.11, "Segmented peach") is shown on the next page (p.349).

paragraphs.what_it_says: A one-line transition: the point shown in Figure 11.10 is now passed to SAM as a prompt, in the code block that follows.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Up to now the point was only drawn on the image with `show_points`. Here it becomes an actual model input, together with its label (1 = foreground) and the image itself.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It marks the shift from preparation (p.345-347) to inference. Note that no training happens: `model.predict` runs the pretrained SAM weights downloaded in 11.3.1.
paragraphs.technical_idea: `model.predict` accepts a dict of named inputs; the keys must match the model's input names (`images`, `points`, `labels`, and later `boxes`).

terminology.meaning: Extra input that tells SAM which object to segment: here a labeled point; on p.351 a box.
Keras inference method: runs the forward pass in batches and returns NumPy-compatible outputs.

connections: p.347: input_point = np.array([[580, 450]]) and input_label = np.array([1]) are defined there.
p.344: the prompt encoder maps points/boxes to embeddings consumed by the mask decoder.

paragraphs.excerpt: The return value `outputs` has a `"masks"` field which contains four
paragraphs.what_it_says: The model returns a dictionary. Its `"masks"` entry holds four 256 × 256 candidate masks for the target object, ranked (per the book) by decreasing match quality; the predicted quality score of each mask is stored in the `"iou_pred"` entry.
paragraphs.what_it_means: SAM does not commit to a single answer. A single point is often ambiguous (does a point on a shirt mean the shirt, the person, or a logo on the shirt?), so the decoder proposes several masks plus a self-estimate of how well each one matches the intended object. That self-estimate is a predicted Intersection-over-Union with the (unknown) true mask. The masks are at 256 × 256, a quarter of the 1024 × 1024 input resolution, so they must be upsampled before overlaying.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Knowing that there are several candidates and a score per candidate lets you (a) pick the best one automatically using `iou_pred`, and (b) look at alternatives when the first one is not what you wanted, as the book does with the banana on p.350.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in the SAM paper the mask decoder has separate output tokens for one 'single-mask' prediction and three 'multimask' predictions, and an IoU-prediction head trained to regress the IoU between each predicted mask and the ground truth. The raw mask values are logits, which is why `get_mask` thresholds them at 0. Whether the four candidates are actually sorted by score in KerasHub should be checked against `iou_pred` (see review flag).

terminology.meaning: One of several alternative segmentations the model proposes for the same prompt.
Model output with one predicted IoU score per candidate mask (shape (1, 4) here), an estimate of mask quality.
Intersection over Union: area of overlap divided by area of union of two masks; 1 = perfect match, 0 = no overlap.

connections: p.340: IoU is introduced as the evaluation metric for the from-scratch segmentation model.
p.350: the other three candidates are plotted for the banana prompt.

concepts.name: Segment Anything Model (SAM)
concepts.definition: A pretrained promptable segmentation model from Meta AI: given an image and a prompt (point or box), it returns masks for the indicated object.
concepts.intuition: Instead of being trained for a fixed list of classes, SAM answers the question 'what object is at this spot?' for any image.
concepts.technical: Image encoder produces an image embedding once; a lightweight prompt encoder embeds points/boxes; a mask decoder combines both to output several mask logits plus predicted IoU scores (p.344-345).
concepts.significance: It lets you segment arbitrary objects without any training, which the book later notes makes it useful for building annotated datasets quickly (p.352).
concepts.example: Point (580, 450) with label 1 → a mask covering the peach (Figure 11.11).
concepts.misconception: SAM does not output class labels: it tells you where an object is, not what it is.

concepts.name: Point prompt
concepts.definition: A set of (x, y) pixel coordinates with labels (1 = foreground, 0 = background) that indicates which object SAM should segment.
concepts.intuition: Like clicking on an object in an image editor's 'magic select' tool.
concepts.technical: Passed as `points` with shape (batch, num_points, 2) and `labels` with shape (batch, num_points). Here (1, 1, 2) and (1, 1).
concepts.significance: The cheapest possible annotation: one click per object.
concepts.misconception: Coordinates are (x, y) = (column, row) in the padded 1024 × 1024 frame, not (row, column) and not in the original photo's pixel grid.

concepts.name: Intersection over Union (IoU)
concepts.definition: Overlap between two masks divided by the area covered by either; ranges from 0 to 1.
concepts.intuition: How much of 'what you drew' and 'what was there' coincide, relative to everything either of them covers.
concepts.technical: SAM's `iou_pred` is a learned regression of this quantity between each candidate mask and the true mask; at inference there is no ground truth, so it is a self-assessment.
concepts.significance: Lets you rank or filter candidate masks automatically.
concepts.example: Predicted mask of 900 px, true mask of 1000 px, overlap 850 px → IoU = 850 / (900+1000-850) = 850/1050 ≈ 0.81.
concepts.misconception: `iou_pred` is not a measured IoU; it is the model's guess and can be wrong.

concepts.name: Thresholding mask logits
concepts.definition: Turning real-valued per-pixel scores into a boolean mask by comparing them to a threshold, here 0.0.
concepts.intuition: Positive score = 'this pixel belongs to the object', negative = 'it does not'.
concepts.technical: If the values are logits z, then sigmoid(z) > 0.5 is equivalent to z > 0, so `> 0.0` is the natural decision boundary.
concepts.significance: Required before the mask can be used for display, area measurement or as a training label.
concepts.misconception: Thresholding before resizing would give blocky edges; the book resizes first (bilinear interpolation of the logits) and thresholds afterward.

concepts.name: Batch axis
concepts.definition: The leading dimension of a model input that indexes independent samples.
concepts.intuition: Models are built to process stacks of examples, so a single example must be wrapped in a stack of one.
concepts.technical: `ops.expand_dims(image, axis=0)` turns (1024, 1024, 3) into (1, 1024, 1024, 3); the output masks keep it as the first axis of (1, 4, 256, 256), which is why `get_mask` indexes `[0]`.
concepts.significance: Shape mismatches here are the most common error when calling a pretrained model on one sample.
concepts.misconception: The batch axis is not optional even for a single image.

math.title: Intersection over Union (what iou_pred estimates)
math.source_text: The quality scores of the masks are available under the "iou_pred" field (IoU itself defined in words on p.340: intersection area divided by union area)

variables.meaning: Set of pixels in the predicted mask
Set of pixels in the ground-truth mask of the intended object
Number of pixels in a set

math.operations: Count overlapping pixels, count pixels in either mask, divide.
math.purpose: Measures how well a mask matches the target object; SAM's iou_pred head predicts this number for each of its four candidates.
math.interpretation: 1 means a perfect match, 0 a complete miss (p.340).
math.intuition: Both missing pixels and extra pixels lower IoU, because extra pixels enlarge the union and missing pixels shrink the intersection.
math.numerical_example: If a candidate mask covers the peach plus part of the neighbouring apple: $|A|=1200$, $|B|=1000$, $|A\cap B|=980$ → IoU $= 980/(1200+1000-980) = 980/1220 \approx 0.80$.

math.title: Why the threshold is 0.0

variables.meaning: Mask value (logit) at pixel row i, column j after resizing
Boolean mask value at that pixel

math.purpose: Converts continuous logits into a binary mask.
math.interpretation: A pixel is in the mask when the model's implied probability of membership exceeds 50%.
math.intuition: The sigmoid crosses 0.5 exactly at z = 0, so no sigmoid needs to be computed.

code.title: Running SAM on the point prompt
code.what_it_does: Runs a forward pass of the pretrained SAM on one image with one labeled point and stores the dictionary of outputs.

line_explanations.explanation: `model` is the KerasHub SAM loaded in 11.3.1; `predict` runs inference.
The padded 1024 × 1024 × 3 image from `resize_and_pad` (p.346) gets a batch axis → (1, 1024, 1024, 3).
`input_point` of shape (1, 2) (one point, x and y) → (1, 1, 2): batch, number of points, coordinates.
`input_label` of shape (1,) → (1, 1): one label per point, 1 = foreground.
The inputs are passed as a dict keyed by the model's input names.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: images (1, 1024, 1024, 3), points (1, 1, 2), labels (1, 1). Output: dict containing "masks" (1, 4, 256, 256) and "iou_pred" (one score per candidate).
code.algorithm: Image encoder → image embedding; prompt encoder → point embedding; mask decoder → 4 mask logits + 4 predicted IoUs.
code.theory_link: Promptable segmentation (p.344-345): the model was trained on (image, prompt, mask) triples where point prompts were random pixels inside a mask.

parameters.name: labels
parameters.role: Foreground (1) / background (0) flag for each point

pitfalls: Forgetting `expand_dims` gives shape errors: every input needs the batch axis.
Points must be expressed in the padded 1024 × 1024 frame, not the original photo's resolution.
Points are (x, y) = (column, row), the Matplotlib convention used by `show_points`.

# AI-written: pick the candidate SAM itself scores highest
scores = outputs["iou_pred"][0]          # shape (4,)
best = int(np.argmax(scores))
print(scores, "-> best candidate:", best)
mask = get_mask(outputs, index=best)

code.title: Checking the shape of the mask output
code.what_it_does: Prints the shape of the predicted masks.

line_explanations.explanation: Access the "masks" entry of the output dict.

code.theory_link: The decoder works on a 4× downsampled grid relative to the 1024 × 1024 input, so masks must be upsampled for display.
pitfalls: The masks are not at the image resolution; overlaying them directly would mis-align by a factor of 4.

code.title: get_mask helper and its first use
code.original_code:
def get_mask(sam_outputs, index=0):
    mask = sam_outputs["masks"][0][index]
    mask = np.expand_dims(mask, axis=-1)
    mask = resize_and_pad(mask)
    return ops.convert_to_numpy(mask) > 0.0

mask = get_mask(outputs, index=0)
code.what_it_does: Extracts one candidate mask, upsamples it to the 1024 × 1024 image frame and returns it as a boolean NumPy array; then extracts candidate 0.

line_explanations.explanation: `index` selects which of the four candidates to return (default the first).
`[0]` drops the batch axis, `[index]` picks a candidate → (256, 256).
Adds a channel axis → (256, 256, 1), the image-like layout `ops.image.resize` expects.
`resize_and_pad` (p.346) resizes to (1024, 1024, 1). The mask is already square, so no padding is added; it simply aligns with the padded image.
Converts the backend tensor to NumPy and thresholds at 0 → boolean array (1024, 1024, 1).
Gets the first candidate for the peach prompt; it is drawn on the next page.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: SAM outputs dict and a candidate index. Output: boolean array of shape (1024, 1024, 1), which is the shape `show_mask` (p.347) unpacks as `h, w, _`.
code.algorithm: select → add channel → bilinear resize → threshold.
code.theory_link: Resizing the logits before thresholding gives smoother mask edges than resizing a binary mask.

parameters.name: index
parameters.role: Which of the 4 candidates (0-3) to extract

pitfalls: Only the first batch element is ever returned (`[0]` is hard-coded).
Reusing `resize_and_pad` works here only because the mask is square and the image was already padded to a square; for a non-square mask the padding would be different.
The trailing channel axis is required because `show_mask` does `h, w, _ = mask.shape`.

deeper.title: Following the shapes through one SAM call
deeper.body:
1. `image`: (1024, 1024, 3) → `expand_dims` → (1, 1024, 1024, 3).
2. `input_point`: (1, 2) → (1, 1, 2). `input_label`: (1,) → (1, 1).
3. SAM returns `masks`: (1, 4, 256, 256) and (beyond the shapes printed in the book) `iou_pred`, one score per candidate.
4. `masks[0][0]`: (256, 256) → `expand_dims(-1)`: (256, 256, 1) → `resize_and_pad`: (1024, 1024, 1) → `> 0.0`: boolean (1024, 1024, 1).

Each stage either adds/removes a size-1 axis or changes resolution; nothing mixes pixels across objects.

deeper.title: Why several masks for one click?
deeper.body: If someone points at a button on your coat and says 'that', they might mean the button, the coat, or you. SAM is in the same position with a single point, so it returns several plausible answers at different granularities and a confidence for each. The banana example on p.350 shows this: some alternatives cover one banana, others both.

deeper.title: Using iou_pred instead of always taking index 0
deeper.body: The book always takes the first candidate. In an automatic pipeline (for example, the dataset-building use case mentioned on p.352) you would typically pick `argmax(iou_pred)` or drop masks whose predicted IoU is below a threshold. See the illustrative code on code item c1. Not in the book.

misconceptions.claim: SAM returns one mask the same size as the input image.
misconceptions.correction: It returns four candidate masks at 256 × 256, which must be resized to the 1024 × 1024 frame (via resize_and_pad) before overlaying.

misconceptions.claim: `iou_pred` is the true IoU of each mask.
misconceptions.correction: It is the model's own prediction of IoU; no ground truth is available at inference.

misconceptions.claim: The mask values are probabilities, so the threshold should be 0.5.
misconceptions.correction: The book thresholds at 0.0, which corresponds to treating the values as logits (sigmoid(0) = 0.5).

misconceptions.claim: A single image and a single point can be passed without a batch axis.
misconceptions.correction: Every input needs the leading batch dimension, which is why each array is wrapped in ops.expand_dims(..., axis=0).

takeaways: SAM point prompts are passed as a dict with images, points and labels, each with a leading batch axis.
The output "masks" has shape (1, 4, 256, 256): four low-resolution candidate masks per prompt.
"iou_pred" holds the model's predicted IoU for each candidate, a quality estimate you can use to choose among them.
get_mask selects a candidate, adds a channel axis, resizes it to the padded 1024 × 1024 frame and thresholds at 0.
Masks must be mapped into the same coordinate frame as the image (same resize_and_pad) to overlay correctly.

questions.question: What does the shape (1, 4, 256, 256) of outputs["masks"] mean?
options: 4 images in the batch, each with a single 256 × 256 mask
questions.explanation: The page states the field contains four 256 × 256 candidate masks; the leading 1 is the batch axis added with expand_dims. There are no color channels in a mask, SAM gives no classes, and only one image was passed.

questions.question: Why is each input wrapped in ops.expand_dims(..., axis=0)?
questions.answer: To add a batch axis of size 1, because the model processes batches of images and prompts.
questions.explanation: image (1024,1024,3) → (1,1024,1024,3); points (1,2) → (1,1,2); labels (1,) → (1,1). The output keeps that batch axis, hence the [0] in get_mask.

questions.question: Why does get_mask call resize_and_pad on the mask instead of overlaying the 256 × 256 mask directly?
questions.answer: The mask is at a quarter of the input resolution; resizing it to 1024 × 1024 puts it in the same coordinate frame as the padded image so pixel positions line up.
questions.explanation: The image shown in the figures is the 1024 × 1024 padded output of resize_and_pad (p.346). A 256 × 256 mask drawn on it would cover only the top-left quarter. Using the same function guarantees identical framing; padding is a no-op because the mask is square.

questions.question: A candidate mask has 1,200 pixels, the true object has 1,000 pixels, and they overlap on 900 pixels. What IoU should an ideal iou_pred head report?
Why does get_mask threshold at 0.0?
options: Because mask values are probabilities and 0.0 is the minimum
Because the values behave like logits, and logit > 0 corresponds to probability > 0.5
Because Matplotlib cannot display negative values
questions.answer: Because the values behave like logits, and logit > 0 corresponds to probability > 0.5
questions.explanation: With probabilities, thresholding at 0 would include almost every pixel. The padding value and Matplotlib are unrelated to the decision boundary. (The logit interpretation is an explanation beyond the book's text.)

questions.question: Why would a promptable segmentation model return several candidate masks rather than one?
questions.answer: A single point is ambiguous: it can belong to nested objects or parts. Returning several masks with quality scores lets the user or a program pick the intended one.
questions.explanation: The book shows this on p.350-351, where alternatives for the banana prompt include both bananas.

questions.question: Without looking, can you write get_mask and state the shape after each line?
questions.explanation: If you can reproduce this, you can adapt SAM's output to any display or downstream use.
